messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

Quick one: Two-stage rocket: Cesaroni O3400 booster, Cesaroni M2045 sustainer. Design a rocket that goes about 8,000 m. Booster and sustainer both land under 5 m/s. It usually blows around 2 m/s at our field. Show me what you've got.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: Two-stage, motors fixed. Booster is a Cesaroni O3400. Sustainer is a Cesaroni M2045. Apogee about 8,000 m, within 5%. Both sections land under 5 m/s (maximum). Wind about 2 m/s, so I will fly at 2 m/s. Rail and site are not stated: 1.5 m vertical rail, sea level.

2. Feasibility: 8,000 m drag-free needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 8000) = 396 m/s at burnout, and drag will take a large cut, so these motors only work in a narrow, light-for-their-class airframe. An O plus an M may also bump into the 40,960 N*s total-impulse ceiling. I need both motors' impulse, thrust, diameter and mass before I size anything.

2. Feasibility: The O3400 is 21,041 N*s, 3,421 N average, 6.14 s, 98 mm, 1.24 m long, loaded mass 16.8 kg. The M2045 is 7,328 N*s, 2,084 N average, 3.51 s, 75 mm, 0.89 m long, loaded mass 6.07 kg. Both are plugged (only a 0 s delay), so each stage needs an apogee chute rather than motor ejection. Total impulse is 21041 + 7328 = 28,369 N*s, under the 40,960 N*s ceiling. On a guessed 30 kg liftoff only the booster is lit, so thrust-to-weight is 3421 / (30 * 9.81) = 11.6. Weight is 30 * 9.81 = 294 N, rail acceleration (3421 - 294) / 30 = 104 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 104 * 1.5) = 17.7 m/s. The 4,700 N spike makes the 1.5 m rail comfortable.

3. Size: Sustainer is the 75 mm stage, booster the 98 mm stage, with a short transition between them. Booster separates at burnout and the M lights then. For landings under 5 m/s I will use a 2.6 m sustainer chute and a 4.0 m booster chute, both at apogee, Cd 0.8. The booster is the heavy piece after it drops the 11 kg of propellant.

4. Draft: Fiberglass airframe, four fiberglass fins on each stage, O3400 in the booster, M2045 in the sustainer, both plugged. Checking it in 2 m/s wind on the 1.5 m rail.

4. Check: The simulator gives 11771.9 m, far above about 8,000 m. (11771.9 - 8000) / 8000 = 47% high. Margin fails at 0.63 cal, both at rail exit and as the burn minimum, against 1.0 cal. Sustainer landing is 5.6 m/s, over the 5 m/s cap, and the flight was cut off at 1199.9 s before that section reached the ground. Booster landing is 4.5 m/s and it did reach the ground. Rail exit 19.9 m/s and thrust-to-weight 10.3 pass. Peak Mach is 3.01, with a supersonic warning, and there is an open-forward-airframe warning on the booster tube. Liftoff mass is 33.8 kg, near the 30 kg guess, so the miss is not a bad mass estimate. It is too little drag and too little fin.

5. Fix: The failing values are apogee 11771.9 m, margin 0.63 cal and sustainer landing 5.6 m/s. The fins are the cause of the first two: the CP is not far enough back, and at Mach 3 the small planform is not spending the impulse. One change: sustainer span to 0.20 m and booster span to 0.28 m, with the chords grown to match. Chutes stay for this pass so I can see the drag effect on its own.
